data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction between 'truly independent' and 'merely appears uncorrelated until a shared cause is found' is not resolvable by any finite evidence, because any observed lack of correlation can be attributed to a sample that does not include the shared cause yet. Therefore, the debate is underdetermined: the choice between centralized redundancy and decentralization should be made on other grounds (e.g., cost, latency, governance), because the key evidentiary question is unanswerable.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a rigorous, closed-form model of all possible shared causes were available and could be empirically tested against, the claim of underdetermination would weaken.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the standard of evidence were relaxed to 'independence with respect to a defined, bounded class of causes', the question becomes resolvable and the claim no longer applies.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The evidentiary standard requires proving a negative (absence of a shared cause) over a space of possible shared causes that is open-ended and includes unknown unknowns (e.g., a new vulnerability class, a novel social phenomenon, an unforeseen regulatory action). No finite observation can rule out all future shared causes. Any apparent independence is conditional on the set of shared causes considered so far; a new shared cause can always be discovered that collapses the observed independence. The question is therefore not merely empirical but epistemological: the kind of evidence requested cannot exist in principle.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
